claims.proposition_evaluated: The City's latest published condition ratings available by 2026-09-03 (the 2025 Infrastructure State and Condition Report) show that Edmonton's asset class published under the City's label for roads ('Roads') had a D (poor) plus F (very poor) share p of at least 25% (Supported), 10% to <25% (Partially supported), or <10% (Contradicted), by replacement value, as of the inventory date those ratings describe.
claims.interpretation_notes: Partially supported under the primary cutoffs. The part of the proposition that holds: a non-trivial share of the City's 'Roads' class is rated D or F. The part that fails: the generality 'the roads are in poor condition', which needs p of 25% or more. The only figure I could find is p = 11.2% (Roads, 2025 report, Appendix B, p. 37). It is in the 10% to <25% band. Alternative cutoffs (Supported 20%+, Partial 7.5% to <20%, Contradicted <7.5%) give the same result: 11.2% is Partially supported. Sub-classes the 2025 report reportedly nests under 'Roads': Paved (reportedly 12.5% D+F), Unpaved (share not recovered), and a Curbs line of about $2.1B at 7% D+F. Following the brief, curbs are kept inside the City's own class and not removed by hand; I report them here as a qualification under the City's label. With curbs, p is 11.2%. Paved alone would be 12.5%, but that is a category I would have assembled, so it is not used. The margin over the 10% boundary is 1.2 percentage points, which is thin given that the figure comes from a transcription. Previous rating (2023 values, reportedly printed beside 2025 in the same appendix): 11.4% D+F, so a -0.2 point change, reported and not judged. The 2020 edition's Roads row (11.0%) was assembled differently: it reportedly included alleys at 64% D+F and had no curbs line. The report itself reportedly says its methodology differs from previous years, so the three values are not a like-for-like trend. Excluded classes (bridges, sidewalks, streetlights, transit/LRT, buildings, parks) were not examined, because the report itself could not be opened.

supporting_evidence.finding: A third-party transcription of the 2025 ISC report's Appendix B (p. 37) gives the 'Roads' D+F share as 11.2% for 2025 on a replacement value of $10,484M, and 11.4% for 2023 on $9,747M. It also gives 2025 Good 70.8% and Fair 16.2%.

claims.proposition_evaluated: Of the $100.0M approved for CM-20-0330 (2023-2026), at least $50.0M (E) came from funding sources whose terms permitted road or alley renewal. General municipal capital funding (tax-supported debt, pay-as-you-go, unrestricted reserves) counts as eligible unless the record says otherwise. Restricted grants count as eligible only if the granting body's published terms permit renewal.
claims.interpretation_notes: Not established, as a finding about what I could reach, not about what the City publishes. The profile sheet for CM-20-0330 in the adopted 2023-2026 Capital Budget (which carries the funding sources) could not be read: the PDF text was not extractable by my tool, and all eSCRIBE council documents returned HTTP 403. No primary document I reached gives a dollar breakdown of funding sources, so U = $100.0M, E = 0, X = 0, which falls in the Not established band under both cutoff sets. The leads point strongly one way. Taproot reported that in the 22 Nov 2023 deliberations the mover of a motion to halve the programme said it was financed through tax-supported debt, and that administration quantified tax-supported debt savings of $123,000 (2024), $776,000 (2025) and $1.9M (2026) from a $50M cut. Tax-supported debt is general municipal capital funding, so it is eligible under this brief. If the profile sheet confirms that the programme is at least half tax-supported debt or pay-as-you-go, E is $50M or more and the verdict becomes Supported under both cutoffs. The brief bars a news report from being the source of a figure in a verdict, so I have not classified on these leads. The story must not use the Stakes line 'Edmonton does not publish enough' on the strength of this review. That would convert an access failure into a claim about the record. I found no restricted grant tied to CM-20-0330. The federal Active Transportation Fund contribution of $8.9M in April 2023 was announced for other named projects (Jasper Avenue and planning studies), and I found no link to this profile.

supporting_evidence.finding: 22 Nov 2023: Coun. Principe (seconded by Coun. Rice) moved to halve the $100M. She said the aim was to minimize tax-supported debt. Administration said the cut would save $123,000 (2024), $776,000 (2025) and $1.9M (2026) in tax-supported debt. The motion was defeated; Principe, Cartmell and Hamilton were in favour.

claims.proposition_evaluated: $100M is at least 0.25 (Supported), 0.05 to <0.25 (Partially supported) or <0.05 (Contradicted) of S. S is the City's own published unfunded renewal figure covering the 2023-2026 capital budget cycle, across all its assets.
claims.interpretation_notes: Partially supported. The part that holds: the $100M is a real fraction of the City's 2023-2026 renewal shortfall. The part that fails: 'serious share' (r of 0.25 or more). The City figures for 2023-2026 I could reach, all through search excerpts of City reports that returned 403 when opened: (a) the Spring 2024 Supplemental Capital Budget Adjustment says 'in the originally approved 2023-2026 Capital Budget, the ideal renewal investment was identified as $3.5 billion; however, funding available for renewal was only 54 per cent of this ideal requirement'. By my arithmetic the unfunded part is $3.5B x 0.46 = about $1.61B; the excerpt does not show the City printing that dollar figure. (b) FCS02696 (City Council, June 10, 2025) says '$2.06 billion is allocated to the ideal renewal investment' of a $9.44B approved budget, and CBC reported this report as finding a $1.5B shortfall for 2023-26. (c) The City's budget FAQ, reported via search, puts ideal renewal needs over 2023-2026 at 'about $3.6 billion'; $3.6B - $2.06B = $1.54B. r = 100/1,610 = 0.062; 100/1,540 = 0.065; 100/1,500 = 0.067. Each lands in the Partially supported band under the primary cutoffs (0.05 to 0.25) and under the alternative cutoffs (0.03 to 0.15). The classification only changes if S is at or below $400M or above $2.0B (primary), or at or below $667M or above $3.33B (alternative), and no City figure for 2023-2026 is near those values. The difference figures are subtractions of two City figures on the same basis, not rescaled figures. I could not read the City's own heading for the difference on pp. 42-49 of the capital budget. Longer-span figures, reported and not classified: the 10-year gap of $4.8B (2023-2032 Capital Investment Outlook, June 2022, reported via search), r = 0.021; the roughly $10B 10-year gap (2026 outlook), r = 0.010. Both are different periods and are not classified.

supporting_evidence.finding: The originally approved 2023-2026 Capital Budget identified ideal renewal investment of $3.5B, with funding available for renewal at only 54% of it. Once constrained programs (e.g. Neighbourhood Renewal) and bridges are set aside, the remainder was funded at about 30.7% of ideal. Read via search excerpt; direct fetch returned 403.
